Finding the Other Half

At a large excavation, thousands of pottery fragments may emerge from separate soil layers. Two pieces that once belonged to the same vessel can be stored in different trays. Comparing every broken edge by hand would take months.

After a fragment is cleaned[1] a scanner records the curves, thickness, and angle of its broken edge. Software converts those measurements into a three-dimensional profile. The fragment's excavation location remains attached to the profile, allowing a confirmed join to connect evidence from two contexts.[2]

When a new profile enters the database, the program celebrates[3] possible matches according to the similarity of their edges. A sequence of measurements along each edge provide[4] more evidence than a comparison of color alone. Researchers inspect the highest-ranked candidates and test a physical join only when handling the pieces is safe.

A digital match cannot prove that two fragments touch; erosion may create deceptively similar curves. It can, however, reduce an enormous search to a practical group of candidates. The final judgment still depends on the fit, material, decoration, and archaeological context of the original pieces.[5]
